Grid and refinement of the sweep

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-reverse-checks.Rmd
methods-reverse-checks.Rmd

The reverse mode of cppODE() differentiates on the value-run grid; where that grid does not resolve the linearized flow, refine holds the sweep to the tolerances. Symbols follow the notation table. Used from R through adjointControl() (refine, gradtol, trace) as adjoint of solveODE(), and sensErrCon.

Internal numerical differentiation

In Bock’s internal numerical differentiation [1], [2] the nominal run adapts freely and the selected step sizes are constants of the differentiated scheme. For the result \(y_h(\theta)\) on the grid selected at \(\theta\), \[ \frac{\mathrm{d} y_{h}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial \theta} + \sum_{k} \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial h_{k}}\, \frac{\mathrm{d} h_{k}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} , \tag{1} \] it computes the first term. The grid effect, the sum, is \(O(\mathrm{tol})\) and left out; differentiating the control law to obtain it makes the discrete adjoint inconsistent with the adjoint ODE [3], [4]. Step sizes are smooth in \(\theta\) within an acceptance region and jump where an accepted step turns rejected and the later grid shifts. Automatic differentiation of the control law misses these jumps, which dominate the grid effect, and returns the derivative of neither the exact solution nor the reported value.

Grids of the forward and reverse modes

Each mode returns the state it integrated and the derivative of the scheme that produced it.

  • Forward, default sensErrCon = TRUE: the error norm is the maximum over the sensitivity columns, Forward (4), since their errors accumulate (as CVodeSetSensErrCon). The grid is finer and the values differ from a value run by \(O(\mathrm{tol})\).
  • Reverse: the value pass takes the value-run grid, as the forward run of the CVODES adjoint does, so the gradient is the derivative of the trajectory a value run returns.

Unresolved linearized flow

The step-map derivative is accurate where the step resolves the flow on the tangent modes; the state error measures only the state modes, weighted by the state magnitude. On a trajectory at rest (an undriven state at zero, a steady state) the corrector is exact, the error estimate is zero, the step grows by the maximum controller factor, and the adjoint is the exact derivative of a scheme far from the flow. For \(\dot x = -k x\), \(\dot y = k x - y\) from \(x = y = 0\) with outputs at \(0, 1, \ldots, 50\), the bdf value pass takes three steps and the derivative of \(\sum_o y(t_o)\) in \(y(0)\) is \(4.84\); the flow, returned by refine, gives \(1.58\). Internal numerical differentiation fails the same way for \(\dot x = p x\) from \(x = 0\) [2, Sec. 6.7.5], as does forward automatic differentiation through an adaptive solver whose controller norm omits the derivative parts [5].

Related cases, resolved by refining the sweep, not by the value pass:

  • a state small against \(\mathtt{abstol}/\mathtt{reltol}\), a weaker effect of the same kind;
  • a parameter the state does not see: in \(\dot x = -k x + \sin(100 t)\, u\) at \(u = 0\) the state is smooth while \(\partial x/\partial u\) follows the fast forcing;
  • a parameter entering only through an event value, which acts on the flow from that event on.

Refining the sweep

adjointControl(refine = TRUE) holds each step of the sweep to the tolerances, on the stored trajectory, with the local error test of the CVODES backward problem [6], so a tolerance means the same for both. Step \(n\) passes \(\lambda(t_n)\) down and adds \(\Delta\bar\theta_n\) to the running gradient \(\bar\theta(t_n)\), the sum from the end of the run down to \(t_n\). With \(\delta\) the error estimate of the step adjoint, the step passes when \[ \begin{gathered} \max\Bigl(\bigl\|\delta\lambda(t_n)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{rms},\,w_\lambda},\; \bigl\|\delta\Delta\bar\theta_n\bigr\|_{\mathrm{rms},\,w_\theta}\Bigr) \le 1, \\ w_{\lambda,i} = \mathtt{reltol}\,|\lambda_i(t_n)| + \mathtt{abstol}, \qquad w_{\theta,i} = \mathtt{reltol}\,|\bar\theta_i(t_n)| + \mathtt{gradtol}, \end{gathered} \tag{2} \] in the norm of Stepping (8). The gradient term enters only with gradtol, an absolute tolerance, as CVODES holds the quadrature (CVodeSetQuadErrConB). The test is local: step errors add up over the sweep.

One-step methods. An rb4 step returns \(X_6 + e\), the embedded solution plus the error term of the sixth solve. One more backward pass over the same stages and factorization, seeded on \(e\) alone, estimates the error of the embedded adjoint. A step meeting (2) with it is kept; otherwise it is redone from the start state in \(m = 2, 4, \ldots, 1024\) substeps, forward and back with the observations in each, comparing successive refinements. The difference \(d_m\) is divided by Richardson’s factor \(\min\bigl(2^q - 1,\; \max(1,\, d_{m/2}/d_m - 1)\bigr)\) only as far as two successive differences show the order \(q\), the first halving at face value. tsit5, without embedded adjoint, starts with the halving. adjointControl(trace = TRUE) reports the \(m\) of every step in $adjoint$substeps.

Multistep methods. The Nordsieck array couples a bdf or adams step to the history at order one, so substeps would change what every later step reads. The refined sweep instead integrates the flow adjoint over each grid interval from the stored start state, passing only the state cotangent across grid points. Like the continuous adjoint of CVODES [6], the result, the flow derivative along the computed trajectory, is \(O(\mathrm{tol})\) from the scheme derivative.

The flow over an interval of length \(H\) is extrapolated linearly implicit Euler, the scheme of SEULEX [7, Sec. IV.9]. Chain \(j\) takes \(n_j = j\) steps of \(h_j = H/n_j\), \[ \bigl(h_j^{-1} I - J_0\bigr)\, D_k = f(x_k, t_k), \qquad x_{k+1} = x_k + D_k, \tag{3} \] with \(J_0\) the Jacobian at the interval start. As a W-method, consistent for any matrix in place of the Jacobian, a chain has an error expansion in powers of \(h_j\), and the Aitken-Neville tableau \(T_{j,k} = T_{j,k-1} + (T_{j,k-1} - T_{j-1,k-1}) / (n_j/n_{j-k} - 1)\) raises the order by one per column. Chain \(j\) costs one factorization of \(h_j^{-1} I - J_0\) (a diagonal change of one Jacobian), \(n_j\) right-hand sides and \(n_j\) solves.

\(T_{j,j}\) is a fixed linear combination of the chain end states, so the tableau is built on the chain adjoints (start-state cotangent and interval gradient share), each swept back on the factorization of that chain. A step of (3) passes \(\mu_k = (h_j^{-1} I - J_0)^{-\mathsf T} \lambda_{k+1}\) to \(x_k\) through \(J(x_k)^{\mathsf T} \mu_k\), to \(\theta\) through \((\partial f/\partial\theta)(x_k)^{\mathsf T} \mu_k\), and through \(J_0\) to the start of the interval: \(\sum_k \mu_k^{\mathsf T} (\partial J_0)\, D_k\) is one bilinear form over the Jacobian pattern, \(B_{rc} = \sum_k \mu_{k,r} D_{k,c}\), pulled back by the generated code in one evaluation. \(e_j = T_{j,j} - T_{j,j-1}\) estimates the error of \(T_{j,j-1}\); the returned \(T_{j,j}\) has the error estimate \(e_j \min(1, e_j/e_{j-1})\), the rate of the last two differences applied one column on, as CVODES estimates the error of the solution it returns. The first column passing (2) is taken. An interval failing at the eighth column is halved, and an observation inside an interval cuts it; the new piece starts from the state reached forward under the state error test.

Limits. A one-step step takes at most 1024 substeps, fewer where from \(m = 32\) on a halving no longer shrinks the difference; a multistep interval is halved at most ten times. An error source the refinement does not reduce, such as a forcing far faster than the steps, leaves the estimate below the error.

Value correction of the refined sweep

The refined sweep replaces each step or interval by the map whose adjoint passed the test, linearized at the stored states. With the observation seeds \(w_o\) it differentiates \(J = \sum_o w_o^{\mathsf T} x(t_o)\), whose first-order change equals that of a nonlinear \(L\) with \(w_o = \partial L/\partial x(t_o)\). A refined solve returns this change per seed column as $correction, \[ C = \sum_n \Bigl[\lambda_{n+1}^{\mathsf T}\bigl(\tilde\Phi_n(x^h_n) - x^h_{n+1}\bigr) + \sum_{t_o \in (t_n, t_{n+1}]} w_o^{\mathsf T}\bigl(\tilde x(t_o) - y_o\bigr)\Bigr], \tag{4} \] with \(x^h_n\) the stored states, \(\tilde\Phi_n\) the accepted map of step \(n\), \(\lambda_{n+1}\) the cotangent from the step above, \(y_o\) the value returned at \(t_o\), and \(\tilde x(t_o)\) the accepted map there: the dense output of the substep containing \(t_o\), or for a multistep interval the state at the cut at \(t_o\). A halved interval adds the cotangent-weighted defect of the left half against the midpoint the right half was linearized at. Value plus \(C\) equals the functional of the differentiated trajectory up to terms quadratic in the defects.

At an event the cotangent at the step end is zero; the jump passes the cotangent down as an observation at the stored pre-jump state, so (4) includes the defect of the state entering the jump. Post-jump rows and the initial state have no defect. For a linear model the accepted maps are linear and the sums telescope: value plus \(C\) equals \(x_0^{\mathsf T}\bar x_0\) to rounding, for every method, with or without halving; the tests use this identity.

An unrefined step, such as an rb4 step whose embedded adjoint passes, adds no defect. The corrected value is the value of the function whose gradient is returned, not necessarily closer to the exact objective: with every step substepped it moves a coarse value toward the converged one, and with substepped maps less accurate than the value pass (tight tolerances, smooth problems) it can move away by \(O(\mathrm{tol})\).
